title: Directed Reading
body:
Directed Reading was a senior project: four people, one term, asking how statistical concepts are
actually applied in finance. It produced two things, a working dashboard that computes and
explains risk measures for any traded stock, and a research report on how emotion moves
markets.

The two halves answer the same question from opposite directions. The software half takes the
position that a price series is data and that the right summary statistics describe risk
honestly, which is [[STATISTICS]] applied to a live dataset. The research half documents the
cases where prices moved for reasons no statistic captures, driven by fear, narrative and the
speed at which a platform spreads both.

The software is a Python dashboard built on Shiny, pulling market data, computing
[[Volatility]] and the [[Sharpe Ratio]] over user-selected windows, plotting the results,
and carrying an explanatory panel backed by a language model that is given the computed numbers
so its answers describe the actual stock on screen.

Repository: `github.com/<user>/Machine-Learning-in-Finance-Research`. The report is
`app/Research/Emotional Sentiment/emotional_sentiment_report.tex`, by Alex Melnick, Amtoj
Punia, Andrew Walsh and Evan Wushke, supervised by Jordan Kidney.

## Topics

### Returns, and why the price is the wrong input

Every statistic in the project is computed on [[Financial Returns]]. A price series is not
comparable across stocks, since a $10 move means something different at $20 and at $2000, and
it trends, so its mean and standard deviation describe the trend instead of the variation
around it.

```
100 -> 110      simple return  (110-100)/100 = 0.10, or 10%
```

Converting to daily returns produces a series that is roughly stationary and directly
comparable between assets, which is what makes the mean and the standard deviation meaningful.

### Volatility

[[Volatility]] is the standard deviation of returns, and it is the project's measure of risk.
It is [[Variance]] from [[STATISTICS]] with no modification, applied to a return series, and
the interpretation is the same: the typical distance of a day's return from the average day.

The convention is to report it annualised, which is [[Annualisation]], scaling the daily figure
by $\sqrt{252}$ for the number of trading days in a year:

```
daily standard deviation  1.2%
annualised                1.2% × √252 = 1.2% × 15.875 = 19.05%
```

The square root appears because variances add across independent periods and standard
deviations do not, so scaling the standard deviation means scaling by the square root of the
number of periods. That is the same fact behind the standard error in the
[[Central Limit Theorem]], used in the other direction.

Volatility treats an upward move and a downward move of the same size identically, which is the
honest criticism of it as a risk measure, since investors do not experience them the same way.

### Sharpe ratio

[[Sharpe Ratio]] is the project's central statistic. It measures return per unit of risk,
which is what makes two strategies comparable when one earns more and swings harder:

$$
S = \frac{E[R_p - R_f]}{\sigma_p}
$$

The numerator is the [[Excess Return]], the return above the [[Risk-Free Rate]],
because a return obtainable with no risk should not be credited to a strategy. The denominator
is the volatility above.

```
daily mean excess return   0.032%
daily standard deviation   1.2%
daily Sharpe               0.0267
annualised                 0.0267 × √252 = 0.42
```

The ratio strips out the units, so a number alone is comparable across assets and periods, and
the same $\sqrt{252}$ scaling applies because the numerator scales with time and the
denominator scales with its square root.

Its assumptions are what the dashboard's explanatory text covers. It assumes returns are
roughly symmetric, which market returns are not, since crashes are larger and faster than
rallies. It rewards a strategy with steady small gains and rare catastrophic losses, because
the rare loss barely moves a standard deviation computed over years.

### Rolling windows

A single number computed over ten years hides everything that changed during them. A
[[Rolling Window]] recomputes the statistic over a sliding fixed-length period, producing
a series showing how risk itself moved:

```
window = 60 trading days

day 60:   compute over days   1-60
day 61:   compute over days   2-61
day 62:   compute over days   3-62
```

Plotting rolling volatility against time is how the 2020 crash becomes visible as a spike, and
plotting the rolling Sharpe ratio shows that a strategy's risk-adjusted performance is a moving
quantity and never a fixed property. The window length is the trade: short windows react
quickly and are noisy, and long windows are stable and lag.

### The dashboard

The software half is a [[Shiny]] application in Python, organised as one tab per statistic,
with each tab holding its plots and its explanatory text, and shared modules underneath for
data access, theming and the language model panel.

The structural decision worth noting is that the calculation modules import nothing from the
web framework, which is [[Coupling and Cohesion]] from
[[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]] applied deliberately. The context
builder is pure Python and depends on no library, so it can be tested without starting a server
or fetching any market data, and the repository has unit tests that do exactly that.

[[Containerisation]] handles deployment, with a Dockerfile pinning the Python version and the
dependency set so the application runs the same way on a marker's machine as on the author's.

### Grounding a language model

The explanatory panel is where the two halves of the project meet. A language model asked about
a stock answers from what it absorbed during training, which is generic, possibly stale, and
unconnected to the numbers on the screen.

[[LLM Grounding]] is the technique the project used to fix that. Every computed statistic
is formatted into a plain-text block, and that block is sent with each request, so the model is
answering about the specific ticker, date range and figures the user is looking at:

```
build_stock_context(ticker, company_name, start_date, end_date,
                    period_return_pct, ann_vol_pct, sharpe_ratio,
                    avg_daily_move_pct, best_day_pct, worst_day_pct,
                    trading_days)
```

The engineering around it matters as much as the idea. A per-session call limit caps cost and
abuse, the API key is read from the environment and stays out of the repository, and the system
prompt constrains the model's role and refuses to give financial advice, which is a design
decision about liability as much as about behaviour.

### Emotional sentiment in the market

The research half argues that markets are moved by fear, greed, hype and the stories investors
tell each other, alongside earnings and rates. [[Investor Sentiment]] is the report's term
for that component, and its central claim is that sentiment matters most where valuation is
hardest, so speculative assets are the most emotional ones.

Three mechanisms carry it. [[Herd Behavior]] is buying because others are buying, since
being wrong collectively feels safer than being wrong alone. [[Narrative Contagion]] is
the spread of a story that supplies a reason to expect prices to keep moving. The [[VIX]] is
the market's own measure of expected volatility, treated as a fear gauge.

[[Behavioral Finance]] is the field the report draws on, and its literature supplies the
evidence: sentiment has larger effects on securities that are hard to value and hard to
arbitrage, unusually pessimistic media tone is followed by price pressure and then a rebound,
and attention generated on a retail trading forum is followed by more uninformed trading and
worse holding-period returns.

The fintech angle is what makes the topic current. Sentiment always existed and now travels at
the speed of a notification, and the platforms distribute it and do more than reflect it. The
report's case studies are the 2008 crisis as greed turning to panic, the COVID-19 crash as fear
moving before the fundamentals were known, GameStop as a platform transmitting mood directly
into trading, and crypto cycles as momentum reinforcing itself.

The connection back to the software half is the honest one. A [[Sharpe Ratio]] computed
over a period containing a sentiment-driven crash reports the crash as volatility and says
nothing about why it happened, which is the limitation the two halves of the project were run
to expose.

## Related courses

- [[STATISTICS]] is the whole statistical content, since [[Volatility]] is
  [[Variance]] applied to returns, [[Annualisation]] is the $\sqrt{n}$ scaling behind the
  [[Central Limit Theorem]], and the [[Sharpe Ratio]] is a mean divided by a standard
  deviation.
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]] supplies the vocabulary for the language model half and the warning
  that a model's output is a fit to its training data.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]] supplies the structure, since the
  separation between calculation and presentation is [[Coupling and Cohesion]], and the
  testable pure module is what [[Unit testing]] requires.
- [[WEB DEVELOPMENT FOR CS]] is the same client and server split, where
  [[Server Side]] holds the API key and the [[Client]] holds nothing secret.
- [[INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY AND SOCIETY]] covers the [[FinTech]] questions this
  project met in practice, including who is accountable for an automated financial decision.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE]] is where the Python came from, and
  [[NumPy]] in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] is what the calculations run on.
